strengths: The paper targets an important and practically relevant problem: epidemic forecasting under partial observability and non-stationary dynamics, where naive neural-mechanistic hybrids can indeed fail.

The proposed EpiNode architecture is coherent: decomposing the observed infection signal into trend/seasonal/residual components, extrapolating those controls, and coupling them to bounded SIRS dynamics is a reasonable design for stabilizing long-horizon forecasts.

The empirical section includes a broad set of baselines spanning statistical, sequence, neural ODE, physics-informed, and graph-based models, plus ablations over decomposition method, number of components, separate vs shared latent ODEs, and delay embedding.

The paper is generally well organized and includes an explicit limitations and impact discussion, including the important caveat that individual rates are not identifiable from infection-only observations and that forecasts should not be used as standalone policy tools.
weaknesses: The central interpretability/parameter-recovery claims are not fully supported. Since beta, gamma, and delta are constrained by predefined bounds, reporting that inferred rates stay within ground-truth ranges is weak evidence; more importantly, infection-only SIRS is non-identifiable, and the paper does not provide a convincing statistical treatment of this issue beyond a brief caveat near the end.

Reproducibility is inadequate for an ICML submission. The software/data section says only 'We release the full implementation at' with no URL, and important details are missing or underspecified, including disease-specific parameter bounds, synthetic generation parameters, hyperparameter grids, seed counts, model sizes, training budgets, and baseline tuning protocols.

The evaluation protocol is not fully convincing. Real-data results appear limited to CDC ILI over 2022-2025, with headline plots focused on HHS 4 and aggregate tables whose sample sizes and aggregation over regions/splits are unclear. The paper claims robustness over splits and seeds, but does not report enough experimental design detail to verify this.

Baseline fairness is uncertain. Some strong baselines mentioned in the text, such as TimeKAN and TimeMixer++, are absent from the main RMSE table, while other adapted baselines such as EARTH in a one-node setting may be disadvantaged or not representative of their intended use. Several baselines show near-zero variance, raising questions about stochastic repetition and tuning.

The failure-mode section is useful but mostly qualitative. It presents illustrative plots rather than controlled metrics or diagnostics, so the claimed architectural lessons are suggestive rather than firmly established.

The method has several hand-engineered components whose contribution is hard to disentangle: VMD mode grouping, linear trend extrapolation, seasonal tiling, residual mean filling, lag embedding, bounded rates, and mass correction. Ablations help, but the paper does not adequately test sensitivity to these choices or compare against simpler decomposition-plus-forecaster variants.

The paper overstates significance in places. The method combines known ingredients from decomposition forecasting, neural ODEs, and compartmental modeling; the empirical gains are promising, but the evidence is not strong enough to justify claims of reliable recovery of epidemiological rates or broad applicability across epidemic regimes.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically difficult problem: epidemic forecasting under partial observability and non-stationary dynamics. The motivation is sound, and the discussion of why naive neural-mechanistic hybrids can fail is relevant to the community.

The proposed EpiNode architecture has some reasonable ingredients: explicit multi-scale signal decomposition, bounded epidemiological parameters, SIRS rollouts, and ablations over decomposition choices and latent ODE structure.

The manuscript includes comparisons against several classical, neural, continuous-time, and physics-informed baselines, plus synthetic settings with matched and mismatched compartmental dynamics. The limitations section is relatively candid about single-region deterministic modeling, lack of uncertainty, and weak interpretability of individual rates under I-only supervision.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not convincingly supported. The evaluation is small and highly curated: most evidence comes from a handful of synthetic datasets and CDC ILI data over 2022-2025, with the main table apparently emphasizing one region/setting despite broader regional claims. It is unclear how robust the results are across diseases, time spans, reporting regimes, and real forecasting conditions.

Reproducibility is poor. The paper states 'We release the full implementation at' but provides no URL. Key details are missing or underspecified, including random seed counts, hyperparameter grids and selection protocol, VMD settings, model capacities, optimizer settings, train/validation/test handling, and exact preprocessing. This makes the large reported gains difficult to verify.

The method risks being partly a decomposition-and-extrapolation heuristic rather than a principled learned epidemiological model. Future controls are produced by linear trend extrapolation, seasonal tiling, and residual averaging, so much of the forecast may come from hand-designed time-series extrapolation. The paper does not compare adequately to simple seasonal-naive, decomposition-only, or SIRS-with-extrapolated-rates baselines that would isolate the value of the neural ODE components.

The parameter inference claims are weak. Under I-only observation, SIRS parameters are generally non-identifiable; the paper acknowledges this only late, but still claims recovery of time-varying beta/gamma/delta. Showing that inferred parameters remain within prescribed bounds is not evidence of recovery, since the network is explicitly constrained to those bounds. Quantitative parameter RMSE and uncertainty are not presented prominently enough to justify the interpretability claims.

The failure-mode section is mostly qualitative. It shows selected plots but lacks systematic experimental protocol, metrics, and fair tuning details. Some conclusions, such as bidirectional objectives or physics-informed losses broadly failing, are stronger than the evidence provided.

Baseline fairness is uncertain. Several baselines are adapted in nonstandard ways, EARTH is reduced to a one-node graph despite being designed for spatial settings, and recent epidemic forecasting methods with probabilistic calibration or ensemble approaches are not seriously considered. There is no uncertainty evaluation, which is a major omission for public-health forecasting.

Presentation has inconsistencies and overclaims. Some tables label signed peak errors as RMSE, the 'lowest RMSE on all five datasets' claim masks small and possibly brittle experimental scope, and the paper repeatedly treats smooth bounded inferred rates as interpretable epidemiological quantities without enough validation.

Ethical and deployment discussion is incomplete. The impact statement notes misuse risk, but the method provides deterministic forecasts without calibrated uncertainty, which is especially problematic for public-health decision support. The paper does not evaluate calibration, worst-case behavior, reporting artifacts, or robustness to data revisions.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practically relevant problem: epidemic forecasting under partial observability and nonstationary transmission. The framing around failure modes of naive neural-mechanistic hybridization is useful and helps motivate the proposed design.

EpiNode is a coherent hybrid architecture: causal trend/seasonal/residual decomposition, channel-specific controlled latent ODEs, bounded epidemiological parameter decoding, and SIRS rollout are combined in a way that directly targets multi-wave forecasting and interpretability.

The empirical results are promising. Across synthetic SIRS/SIR/SEIRS settings and CDC ILI data, the method reports consistently lower RMSE than classical, neural, ODE-based, and epidemiology-informed baselines, with especially strong gains on long-horizon and peak-timing metrics.

The paper includes meaningful ablations on decomposition, number of components, time-delay embedding, and separate versus shared latent ODEs. These support the claim that the decomposition-controlled design is not just incidental.

The limitations and impact discussion are unusually candid: the authors acknowledge single-region deterministic dynamics, absence of uncertainty, sensitivity to decomposition choice, and the weak identifiability of individual epidemiological parameters under infection-only supervision.
weaknesses: The central interpretability claim is only partially supported. Bounded parameter trajectories and smooth seasonal patterns do not by themselves establish that beta, gamma, and delta are identifiable or epidemiologically correct, especially when the paper itself notes that infection-only data mainly constrain an effective reproduction quantity rather than individual rates.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript says the implementation will be released but provides no actual link, and key implementation details such as hyperparameter grids, validation protocol, random seed counts, architecture sizes, solver tolerances, and baseline tuning procedures are not specified in enough detail to reproduce the reported numbers confidently.

The real-data evaluation is narrower than the claims suggest. It uses CDC ILI over 2022-2025 and HHS regions, but there is no comparison across multiple diseases, countries, surveillance systems, or major reporting shifts. This limits evidence for broad applicability to epidemic forecasting generally.

The evaluation protocol may favor the proposed method because decomposition order, VMD bandwidth, delay parameters, disease-specific parameter bounds, and split choices are tuned per dataset. The paper should more clearly separate validation from test selection and quantify sensitivity to these choices.

Some baseline reporting is confusing or incomplete. The text discusses TimeKAN and TimeMixer++, but the main RMSE table does not clearly include both, and adaptations of multi-region or disease-specific baselines such as EARTH and EINN may weaken them relative to their intended use cases.

The failure-mode section is interesting but mostly qualitative. It would be stronger with controlled quantitative diagnostics showing when each hybridization pattern fails, rather than relying mainly on representative plots.

The method depends on extrapolated decomposition channels after the observation window, including linear trend extrapolation and seasonal tiling. This is reasonable but also means part of the forecasting power may come from strong handcrafted seasonal extrapolation rather than the learned neural-mechanistic coupling; the paper could isolate this with stronger decomposition-only and seasonal-naive baselines.
